newsitem.title: USA: Clinton croaks through day with hoarse voice.
newsitem.headline: Clinton croaks through day with hoarse voice.

text.p: President Bill Clinton was forced on Tuesday to turn over some speaking duties to Vice President Al Gore because of a persistent throat problem that has made him hoarse for the last two weeks.

Clinton croaked his way through brief remarks at an Oval Office event on World AIDS Awareness Week, then asked Gore to take over. "As you can tell, the president needs to conserve his vocal chords a little bit," Gore said.
The president was under doctor's orders to rest his voice as much as possible, but a four-day sojourn at Camp David, Maryland, for the Thanksgiving holiday failed to bring a cure.

Aides stressed the president has no problem that cannot be cured with enough rest. Clinton's White House doctor, Connie Mariano, has kept close tabs on him and has recommended he drink hot tea and take throat lozenges in addition to rest.
Still, there was some bafflement as to why his condition has not improved. "He sounded a little worse today than he did yesterday, to me," White House spokesman Mike McCurry said.

Clinton himself jokingly used his throat condition as an excuse not to answer questions about his prospective Cabinet choices for his second term, telling reporters his raspiness was "a hoax" to avoid them.

Aides trace the problem to the long flight from Hawaii to Australia more than two weeks ago. Clinton has long been susceptible to hoarseness and the dry air aboard Air Force One irritated his vocal chords.

By the time of his toast at a state dinner in Bangkok, Thailand, on Nov. 26, Clinton had trouble getting words to come out of his mouth. And during his weekly radio address on Saturday he struggled to speak.

Aides insisted the problem was not interfering with the president's ability to do his work, although McCurry conceded it probably stopped Clinton from making a lot of phone calls over the Thanksgiving holiday about his Cabinet.

"The only thing that he was not able to do over the weekend was to get on the telephone and talk to people. And for those who were at home with their families over Thanksgiving, that was probably just as well anyhow," he said.
Clinton's throat is typically irritated by too much talking and allergic reactions to pollen. He managed to get through his re-election campaign without a voice breakdown, however.
